chapter_summary:
Effective troubleshooting is less about knowing every single command and more about adopting a methodical approach. When a system isn't behaving as expected, the first instinct might be to randomly try solutions, but this often leads to more confusion and wasted time. Instead, a structured methodology, much like the scientific method, provides a clear path. Start by defining the problem precisely: What is happening? When did it start? What changed recently? Is it affecting all users or just some? Is it reproducible? Gathering these initial facts is crucial. Once the problem is defined, formulate a hypothesis about the potential cause. For instance, if a web server isn't responding, a hypothesis could be "the web server service is stopped" or "the firewall is blocking access."

After forming a hypothesis, the next step is to test it. This involves using diagnostic tools and commands to gather evidence. For example, to check if a service is running, you'd use `systemctl status httpd`. If the service is indeed stopped, your hypothesis is confirmed, and you can proceed to restart it. If it's running, your hypothesis is disproven, and you move on to the next most likely cause. This iterative process of hypothesize, test, and analyze continues until the root cause is identified. Always remember to isolate the problem. If a service isn't starting, check its dependencies. Is the network available? Is storage mounted? Are necessary libraries present? Breaking down a complex problem into smaller, manageable pieces makes it much easier to tackle.

One of the most powerful tools for initial diagnosis on a Red Hat system is `journalctl`. This command allows you to query and display messages from the systemd journal, which collects logs from various sources, including the kernel, services, and applications. You can filter `journalctl` output by time (`-S "20 minutes ago"`), by service (`-u httpd`), or by priority (`-p err`). For example, `journalctl -xe` will show you the most recent log entries, including explanatory text and related messages, which is incredibly useful for understanding why a service failed to start. Another invaluable tool is `dmesg`, which displays the kernel ring buffer messages. These messages often contain critical information about hardware detection, driver issues, or kernel panics that occur during boot. Running `dmesg -T` will show timestamps in a human-readable format, helping you pinpoint issues related to system startup.

Beyond logs, understanding process and network state is vital. Commands like `ps aux` provide a snapshot of running processes, allowing you to see which processes are consuming resources or if a critical process is missing. `lsof -i :80` can tell you which process is listening on port 80, useful for diagnosing web server conflicts. For more in-depth process analysis, `strace` can trace system calls and signals, revealing exactly what a program is doing at a low level. While `strace` output can be verbose, it's incredibly powerful for debugging elusive application issues, showing file access, network connections, and library calls.

Ansible plays a significant role in modern troubleshooting by automating the information-gathering phase. Instead of manually logging into multiple servers to run `journalctl` or `dmesg`, you can write a simple Ansible playbook to collect this data centrally. For instance, an ad-hoc command like `ansible all -m shell -a "journalctl -xe --since '1 hour ago'"` can quickly fetch recent log entries from all managed hosts. For more structured data, you can use the `setup` module to gather facts, or custom scripts to extract specific configuration details. A playbook could collect service statuses, network configurations, or even specific log file snippets, storing them on the control node for later analysis. This not only saves time but also ensures consistency in data collection, which is paramount when dealing with distributed systems. Always remember to document your findings and the steps you took. This creates a knowledge base for future issues and aids in communication with team members. A common mistake is to jump to conclusions without sufficient evidence; always verify your assumptions with concrete data. Another pitfall is making changes without a rollback plan. Before implementing a fix, ensure you know how to revert it if it causes new problems.

screens.title: Essential Troubleshooting Methodologies
screens.subtitle: A methodical approach to diagnose Linux system issues using logs, process tools, and Ansible

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn a repeatable way to find and fix Linux system failures. Troubleshooting is a structured activity: define the exact problem, form a hypothesis about the cause, and then test that hypothesis with data. We will show precise commands used on Red Hat systems to inspect service state, system logs, kernel messages, processes, ports, and low-level system calls. You will see how journalctl and dmesg reveal clues about failed services and boot-time issues, while ps, lsof, and strace show process and input and output behavior. We also cover practical use of Ansible to collect the same diagnostic data from many hosts so you can analyze it centrally. Importantly, troubleshooting is not guess-and-change: document your steps, verify assumptions with evidence, and always prepare a rollback plan before applying fixes. A short scenario will tie these ideas together: an intermittent httpd start failure after reboot. By the end of the chapter you will have both a mental workflow and concrete commands to gather evidence, confirm root causes, and share findings with a team.

keyIdea.title: Methodical, evidence-first troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Define the problem, hypothesize, test with logs and commands, and automate data collection with Ansible.

narration.text: By the end of these lessons you will be able to apply a structured troubleshooting workflow to complex Linux issues. You will learn to define problems clearly, form and test hypotheses, and use core tools to gather evidence. Practical commands such as systemctl, journalctl and dmesg will become familiar as diagnostic tools. You will also practice inspecting processes and network state with ps and lsof and learn when to use strace for low-level debugging. Finally, you will see how Ansible can automate data collection across many hosts so you can analyze failures consistently. These skills matter because modern infrastructure is distributed; a single manual check is slow and error prone. The ability to collect consistent, timestamped logs and facts, document what you found, and communicate a rollback-safe fix is what moves incidents from chaos to controlled resolution. Each objective ties to a measurable competency: evidence-based diagnosis, effective use of core utilities, and automated, repeatable collection of diagnostics.

screens.title: The Structured Troubleshooting Loop
screens.subtitle: Define the problem, hypothesize, test, and analyze

narration.text: A systematic troubleshooting loop prevents wasted effort and reduces the chance of introducing new problems. The loop starts with a precise definition: what is failing, when, and who is affected. A vague "it doesn't work" is unhelpful; document exact symptoms and scope. Next, formulate a small set of testable hypotheses that explain the symptoms. For example, for an unresponsive web site a hypothesis could be that the web server process stopped, or that a firewall now blocks port 80. Then test each hypothesis using focused commands: check service state, read recent logs, or confirm port bindings. Testing is evidence gathering: it should either confirm the hypothesis or rule it out. After tests, analyze the results and iterate — either apply a fix when the cause is clear or form a refined hypothesis and test again. A common misconception is to jump to the most convenient fix; avoid changing multiple variables at once. Instead, change one thing, collect new evidence, and document the outcome. Practically, this means running commands like systemctl status, journalctl, and lsof in a disciplined order, capturing output, and preparing a rollback plan before applying corrective changes. How will you make your next troubleshooting step reproducible and reversible?

keyIdea.title: Iterate with focused tests
keyIdea.text: Test hypotheses with targeted commands, one change at a time, and document evidence to confirm root cause.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Structured Loop
Definition
Define → Hypothesize → Test → Analyze

A repeatable loop that turns observed symptoms into verifiable evidence and then into a remediation plan.

  • Define: record exact symptoms, affected hosts, and timeline.
  • Hypothesize: create focused, testable explanations for the failure.
  • Test: run commands to gather supporting or refuting evidence.
  • Analyze: confirm root cause, plan fix, and document rollback options.
Example

If httpd fails after reboot, hypothesize service not started or port taken. Test with systemctl and lsof. Confirm with journalctl and then act.

Key Takeaway

A disciplined loop reduces guesswork: record, test, and only change with a rollback plan.

Annotated steps and commands
Check service state
systemctl status httpd
Confirms whether the unit is active, failed, or inactive and often contains a short journal snippet.
List open sockets
lsof -i :80
Shows which process, if any, is bound to port 80—useful for detecting conflicts.
Read recent logs
journalctl -u httpd -xe
Includes explanatory texts and jumps to the most recent entries to find why a unit failed.
Kernel messages
dmesg -T | tail -n 30
Shows boot and driver-related messages with timestamps for startup issues.
Common mistake: changing configurations before collecting logs. Confirm your hypothesis with targeted commands to avoid unnecessary rollbacks.

screens.title: Define the Problem and Isolate Scope
screens.subtitle: Ask precise questions to narrow the failure domain

narration.text: Effective troubleshooting begins with a precise problem definition and careful isolation of scope. Ask: what is the observable symptom, when did it start, and which users or hosts are affected? Is it reproducible or intermittent? These answers guide which subsystem to inspect first. For example, if a web page returns connection refused on all hosts, the scope may be network or load-balancer related. If a single host shows failure after a reboot, suspect boot, local services, or hardware. Isolation means focusing on one variable at a time: reproduce the problem if possible, try a single control action such as restarting the service on one host, or checking a single port binding with lsof. Capture timestamps and the sequence of events for correlation. A common misunderstanding is to assume all symptoms share a cause—distributed systems often have independent local failures that look similar. By isolating hosts, times, and services you create testable hypotheses and limit blast radius when you make changes. Record what you find; this makes later analysis and team communication faster and prevents repeating the same checks. Define the Problem and Isolate Scope means define affected hosts, times, and reproducibility before testing so each command produces usable evidence.. In practical terms, ask precise questions to narrow the failure domain. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scope narrows successful testing
keyIdea.text: Define affected hosts, times, and reproducibility before testing so each command produces usable evidence.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Define & Isolate
Process
Narrow the scope with targeted questions
  • When did the failure start? Correlate with reboots, deploys, or config changes.
  • Which hosts and users are affected? All or a subset?
  • Is the issue reproducible, intermittent, or one-off?
  • What changed recently: packages, configuration, network, or storage?
Scenario

A single host reports httpd failing after reboot. Since scope is one host, focus on boot logs, dmesg, and local service state before checking network or load balancer.

Misconception

Assuming a repeated symptom across hosts means a single root cause. Independent, local issues can create similar symptoms; isolate to confirm.

Isolation checklist
  1. Reproduce on one host, capture timestamps.
  2. Run systemctl status, journalctl for the unit.
  3. Check dmesg for boot-time errors.
  4. Verify port ownership with lsof.
Pro tip

Use short, reproducible tests and capture outputs to files with timestamps so you can compare before and after changes.

screens.title: Using journalctl Effectively
screens.subtitle: Filter by unit, time, and priority to find relevant messages

narration.text: Journalctl is the go-to tool on systemd-based systems for centralized logs from the kernel, services, and applications. Start by filtering the output to focus on relevant messages: use the unit filter to narrow to a service, a time filter to limit the search window, and a priority filter to see errors first. For example, the command that will be most useful in an immediate failure is the unit-focused view with explanatory text and recent entries. Another helpful variant is a time-limited query that shows all messages since a given interval. When investigating why a unit failed to start, the combination of explanatory text and last entries often reveals permission errors, missing files, or failed dependency checks. A common misconception is that the journal only stores application logs; in reality it aggregates kernel, service, and system messages, which is why using the right filters matters. Always collect the raw output before restarting services so transient error text is not lost. For distributed systems, Ansible can run the same journalctl query across many hosts and centralize the results for easier correlation. How will you choose filters to guarantee you capture the relevant evidence?

keyIdea.title: Filter to find actionable log entries
keyIdea.text: Use unit, time, and priority filters in journalctl to isolate the messages that explain a service failure.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › journalctl
When to use journalctl

Use journalctl to collect unit-specific logs and to read explanatory messages added by services. Apply filters so the output is concise and relevant.

Useful commands
journalctl -u httpd -xe
journalctl --since "20 minutes ago" -p err
journalctl -f -u httpd
The first line filters to the httpd unit with explanatory text and recent entries. The second shows errors since a time window. The third tails live output.
Example

If httpd fails to start, run a time-limited journalctl to capture the error lines that occurred during the attempted start, and save output to a file for analysis.

Notes
  • Use -u to focus on a single service unit.
  • -x adds explanatory text; -e jumps to the end of the journal.
  • Use --since or -S to limit results to a relevant timeframe.
Common mistake

Not filtering the journal makes it hard to find relevant messages. Start narrow, then expand if needed.

screens.title: dmesg and Kernel Diagnostics
screens.subtitle: Use kernel messages to investigate boot and hardware issues

narration.text: Dmesg exposes the kernel ring buffer and is especially useful for startup and hardware-related failures. Kernel messages often include device detection, driver load errors, and filesystem mount failures that occur during boot. When a service fails only after a reboot, dmesg with human timestamps helps correlate hardware or driver problems to the service's failure window. Use the timestamped form to make it easier to align messages with systemctl and journalctl outputs. For example, a sudden failure to mount storage at boot could show up in dmesg as filesystem errors or driver failures. A common misconception is that dmesg is redundant with journalctl—journalctl does include kernel messages, but dmesg is still valuable for a quick, focused look at the kernel buffer and for environments where journal access is restricted. In practice, run dmesg -T and tail the recent lines, capture them to a file, and compare against service logs. This gives you the full picture for root cause analysis when hardware or boot-time events matter. dmesg and Kernel Diagnostics means use dmesg -t to correlate kernel events with service failures, especially after startup or driver changes.. In practical terms, use kernel messages to investigate boot and hardware issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Kernel messages reveal boot and hardware clues
keyIdea.text: Use dmesg -T to correlate kernel events with service failures, especially after startup or driver changes.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › dmesg
Quick commands
dmesg -T | tail -n 50
sudo dmesg -T | grep -i error
The timestamped output is easier to align with journal entries and help identify boot-time hardware or driver failures.
When to use
After reboots, when devices fail to initialize, or when you suspect kernel-level errors affecting services.
Example
A service fails to mount storage at boot; dmesg shows driver timeouts and file system errors at the same timestamp.
Misconception

Assuming dmesg is irrelevant when journalctl exists. Kernel buffers provide immediate startup context and can be viewed even if the journal is inaccessible.

Key Takeaway

Use dmesg to catch boot-time hardware and driver messages that explain service failures shortly after reboot.

screens.title: Inspecting Processes and Ports with ps and lsof
screens.subtitle: Identify missing processes and port conflicts

narration.text: Process and port inspection are essential when a service behaves unexpectedly. The ps command gives you a snapshot of running processes, showing process IDs, resource usage, and the exact command line used to start a process. Use it to confirm that the expected daemon process is present and to find runaway processes consuming C P U or memory. For port conflicts, lsof is the most direct tool: it lists open files including network sockets and reveals which process holds a port. For example, if httpd cannot bind to port 80, lsof -i :80 will show the PID and command holding that socket, so you can decide whether to stop that process or reconfigure the service. A common mistake is to simply restart the expected daemon without checking whether another process already occupies the port; this can produce repeated failures. Combine ps and lsof with systemctl and journalctl: check if the service unit started the correct process, then verify the socket ownership and correlate with journal errors. This combination helps you choose a safe corrective action and a clear rollback if needed.

keyIdea.title: Confirm the expected process and port ownership
keyIdea.text: Use ps to find missing or resource-hungry processes and lsof to detect port ownership and conflicts.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › ps vs lsof
ps: process snapshot
ps aux | grep httpd
Shows processes and their resource usage. Confirm the expected PID and command line flags for the service.
Use ps to discover missing daemons or processes consuming excessive resources that could prevent service startup.
lsof: who owns the socket
lsof -i :80
lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN
Identify which process has bound a port so you can resolve conflicts safely.
Example

If httpd fails to bind port 80 but systemctl shows active, use lsof to see if a different process is already listening. If so, decide whether to stop that process or change the httpd configuration.

Common mistake

Restarting the service without checking port ownership often yields transient success or recurring conflict; always verify the socket is free before binding.

Key Takeaway

Combine ps and lsof with logs to determine whether the expected process is running and which process holds the port.

screens.title: Using strace for Low-Level Debugging
screens.subtitle: Trace system calls to diagnose elusive application failures

narration.text: Strace traces the system calls and signals made by a process, revealing exactly what files, networks, and libraries the process touches. It is particularly helpful when higher-level logs don't explain an application's failure. For instance, if an application fails silently when opening a configuration file, strace will show open attempts, permission errors, or missing file paths. To use it, attach to a running PID or run the process under strace so you capture calls from start. Be aware that strace output can be very verbose; filter for open, read, write, connect, and other system calls relevant to the suspected failure. A common misconception is that strace fixes problems — it does not; it only reveals interactions. Use the information to form a corrective hypothesis, such as missing privileges or incorrect file paths. When using strace in production, limit scope and duration to avoid performance impact. After capturing traces, correlate the system calls with journal entries and process state to build a full picture of the root cause. What system call evidence would confirm your hypothesis about a failing application? Using strace for Low-Level Debugging means use strace to see actual system calls and signals; interpret common errors like enoent or eacces to find root causes.. In practical terms, trace system calls to diagnose elusive application failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trace system calls to expose hidden failures
keyIdea.text: Use strace to see actual system calls and signals; interpret common errors like ENOENT or EACCES to find root causes.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › strace
Common strace patterns
strace -p <PID> -e trace=open,read,write,connect
strace -f -o trace.log <command>
Filter calls to reduce noise. Attach to a running process or start the program under strace to capture startup failures.
Interpreting output
  • ENOENT indicates a missing file or incorrect path.
  • EACCES points to permission issues.
  • Connection failures appear in connect or sendto calls.
Example

An app crashes when reading a config. strace shows open returned ENOENT for the path the app attempts. The fix is to correct the path or place the file where expected.

Caution

strace can slow processes. Limit duration and avoid prolonged tracing on critical production workloads unless you plan for impact.

Key Takeaway

Use strace to convert opaque failures into concrete system call evidence you can act on.

screens.title: Automating Diagnostics with Ansible — Ad-hoc Commands
screens.subtitle: Gather logs and status from many hosts quickly

narration.text: Ansible accelerates the information-gathering phase by executing the same diagnostic commands across many hosts and collecting the outputs centrally. Use ad-hoc commands for quick checks, for example asking all webservers to run a journalctl query or to report systemctl status. This ensures consistent commands, timestamps, and reduces human error from logging into hosts individually. For a failing httpd service, running an ad-hoc shell module that fetches recent journal entries from each host immediately shows patterns and differences across the fleet. A frequent misconception is that automation replaces careful analysis; it does not. Automation simply ensures you gather the same raw evidence consistently and faster. When running Ansible in an incident, ensure you capture outputs to files on the control node and include identifying headers so you can correlate results by host. Also include ignore_errors where appropriate so a single host failure does not stop the collection run. How will you structure your ad-hoc commands to produce timestamped, host-labeled diagnostics? Automating Diagnostics with Ansible — Ad-hoc Commands means use ansible ad-hoc commands to run journalctl, dmesg, and service checks across many hosts and save outputs centrally.. In practical terms, gather logs and status from many hosts quickly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Consistent, fleet-wide evidence collection
keyIdea.text: Use Ansible ad-hoc commands to run journalctl, dmesg, and service checks across many hosts and save outputs centrally.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Ansible Diagnostics
Ad-hoc examples
ansible webservers -m shell -a "systemctl status httpd"
ansible all -m shell -a "journalctl -u httpd --since '1 hour ago' -n 50 --no-pager"
These commands run the same diagnostic on many hosts and return each host's output labeled by inventory name for correlation.
Remember to redirect or copy outputs to the control node for durable storage so you can revisit results later during analysis or share them in a postmortem.
Practical note

Include run_once tasks to create directories on the control node and delegate copy tasks to localhost to gather results consistently.

Common mistake

Stopping collection on the first error. Use ignore_errors or tolerate failures so you gather data from as many hosts as possible.

Key Takeaway

Ansible speeds consistent evidence collection; structure tasks to save outputs with host labels and timestamps for later analysis.

screens.title: Troubleshoot Playbook Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: A repeatable playbook to collect service, journal, and dmesg output

narration.text: A playbook formalizes the diagnostics you would otherwise run interactively, and it stores outputs in a consistent location on the control node. The provided template checks service status, collects the last lines of journalctl for a unit, gathers recent dmesg output, and writes each result to a per-host diagnostics directory. Important details include running tasks with become when needed, using changed_when to prevent altering system state, and delegating file writes to the control node. The playbook also shows the pragmatic use of ignore_errors for tasks that might fail so the run continues and yields data from all hosts. Running such a playbook during an incident gives you an agreed, repeatable set of evidence to inspect, compare, and share. A common pitfall is to include repair steps in the same playbook as data collection; keep collection and remediation separate so you can review findings before making changes. How will you adapt this playbook to include additional checks your environment requires? Troubleshoot Playbook Walkthrough means a playbook can collect service status, journal and dmesg logs from all hosts and save them on the control node for analysis.. In practical terms, a repeatable playbook to collect service, journal, and dmesg output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Collect diagnostics programmatically
keyIdea.text: A playbook can collect service status, journal and dmesg logs from all hosts and save them on the control node for analysis.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Playbook
Troubleshoot playbook (template)
---
- name: Troubleshoot Web Service Issues
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes
  tasks:
    - name: Check httpd service status
      systemd:
        name: httpd
        state: started
      register: httpd_status
      ignore_errors: true

    - name: Gather journalctl output for httpd
      shell: journalctl -u httpd --since "1 hour ago" -n 50 --no-pager
      register: journal_output
      changed_when: false

    - name: Gather dmesg output
      shell: dmesg -T | tail -n 20
      register: dmesg_output
      changed_when: false

    - name: Create diagnostic report directory
      delegate_to: localhost
      file:
        path: "./diagnostics/{{ inventory_hostname }}"
        state: directory
      run_once: true

    - name: Save httpd service status to file
      delegate_to: localhost
      copy:
        content: |
          HTTPD Service Status for {{ inventory_hostname }}:
          -------------------------------------------------
          {{ httpd_status.stdout | default('Service status check failed or service not found.') }}
        dest: "./diagnostics/{{ inventory_hostname }}/httpd_status.txt"
      when: httpd_status is defined

    - name: Save journalctl output to file
      delegate_to: localhost
      copy:
        content: |
          Journalctl Output for httpd on {{ inventory_hostname }}:
          -----------------------------------------------------
          {{ journal_output.stdout }}
        dest: "./diagnostics/{{ inventory_hostname }}/journal_httpd.log"
      when: journal_output is defined

    - name: Save dmesg output to file
      delegate_to: localhost
      copy:
        content: |
          Dmesg Output for {{ inventory_hostname }}:
          ------------------------------------------
          {{ dmesg_output.stdout }}
        dest: "./diagnostics/{{ inventory_hostname }}/dmesg.log"
      when: dmesg_output is defined
This playbook isolates collection and writes per-host diagnostics to the control node for centralized analysis.
Best practices
  • Keep collection and remediation separate.
  • Include run_once and delegate_to for control-node writes.
  • Use changed_when: false for read-only tasks.
Common mistake

Combining fixes with collection can hide whether a repair actually fixed the root cause or introduced new errors. Collect first, then remediate.

screens.title: Root Cause Analysis and Safe Remediation
screens.subtitle: Move from symptom fixes to root cause with documented rollback plans

narration.text: Root cause analysis is the discipline of finding the fundamental reason a problem occurred, not just masking the symptom. After testing hypotheses with logs and process info, examine whether the fix addresses the core issue. For example, restarting a service that failed due to missing mounts will only temporarily restore function; the underlying storage problem must be addressed. Always prepare a rollback plan: backing up configs, noting package versions, and preserving logs so you can undo a change if it causes regressions. Document the evidence, the hypothesis you tested, the commands and outputs, and why the chosen remediation is expected to work. Share this documentation with the team; it shortens incident resolution and supports postmortems. A common error is to assume correlation is causation—confirm that after your fix the original failure path no longer produces the symptom and that no new errors appear in the logs. End with a short verification procedure and a rollback checklist to ensure changes are safe. Root Cause Analysis and Safe Remediation means validate that your remediation addresses the root cause and include a rollback plan and verification steps before applying changes.. In practical terms, move from symptom fixes to root cause with documented rollback plans. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fix the cause, not the symptom
keyIdea.text: Validate that your remediation addresses the root cause and include a rollback plan and verification steps before applying changes.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Root Cause Analysis
Root Cause Checklist
  • Confirm the failing flow and capture logs before any change.
  • Test hypotheses and document commands and outputs for each test.
  • Ensure the chosen fix addresses the evidence collected.
  • Prepare rollback: backups, version pinning, and undo steps.
Verification

After applying a fix, re-run the original diagnostic commands to confirm the symptom no longer occurs and that no new errors appear in journal or dmesg.

Analogy

Treat symptoms like a fever: lowering the temperature is useful, but you should find the infection and treat it to prevent recurrence.

Common mistake

Applying quick fixes without documenting tests and rollback steps often makes later debugging harder and hides recurring root causes.

Key Takeaway

Document evidence, validate fixes, and always have a rollback plan to avoid making incidents worse.

screens.title: Hands-on Scenario: Intermittent httpd Fails After Reboot
screens.subtitle: Apply the loop: define, test with journalctl and dmesg, then collect via Ansible

narration.text: Let's apply the methodology to a concrete scenario: a critical httpd service intermittently fails to start after reboots. First, define the problem: which hosts, precise times, and whether failures are correlated with reboots or deployments. Second, form hypotheses: the service may be failing because the unit didn't start, a port conflict exists, or storage wasn't mounted at boot. Third, test each hypothesis: run systemctl status httpd to see unit state, use journalctl -u httpd -xe to read recent errors, and run dmesg -T to check for boot-time storage or driver errors. If you see a message that the port is in use, run lsof -i :80 to identify the conflicting process. For deeper issues when logs are not clear, attach strace to the process to observe failing system calls. Finally, collect these diagnostics across all webservers with an Ansible playbook that saves service status, journal snippets, and dmesg excerpts to the control node. A common pitfall is restarting services before collecting logs; always gather evidence first. After your tests, confirm the chosen remediation fixes the root cause and that you have a rollback plan.

keyIdea.title: Apply the workflow to a real incident
keyIdea.text: Use systemctl, journalctl, dmesg, lsof, and strace to diagnose and Ansible to collect results across hosts for analysis.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Scenario
Guided terminal steps
1. Confirm unit state
systemctl status httpd
2. Inspect unit logs
journalctl -u httpd -xe
3. Check kernel boot messages
dmesg -T | tail -n 30
Next: collect across hosts
ansible webservers -m shell -a "journalctl -u httpd --since '1 hour ago' -n 50 --no-pager"
This collects the same journal slice from all webservers so you can spot trends or differences quickly.
Check your assumption

If journal entries show missing mounts, fixing the service alone won't help. Confirm that mounts succeed and storage is present before restarting services.

Common mistake

Treating a successful restart as a permanent fix without verifying the root cause leads to recurring incidents.

Key Takeaway

Follow the define-hypothesize-test-analyze loop, collect data across hosts, and verify that the root cause is addressed with a rollback plan ready.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Keep these essential concepts in mind as you troubleshoot: first, use a systematic loop—define the problem, hypothesize, test, and analyze. Second, journalctl is the primary log tool on systemd systems; filter by unit, time, and priority to find actionable messages. Third, dmesg reveals kernel and boot-time messages that often explain post-reboot failures. Fourth, ps and lsof help verify process state and port ownership so you can detect missing daemons or conflicts. Fifth, strace exposes system call-level behavior, essential for hard-to-diagnose application bugs. Sixth, Ansible saves time by collecting the same diagnostics from many hosts and centralizing results. Remember to document your steps, always gather evidence before changing production state, and prepare rollback plans. These habits convert incident response into reproducible, shareable work and reduce recurrence. Which of these practices will you adopt first in your next incident?

keyIdea.title: Keep evidence and automate collection
keyIdea.text: Systematic methods and automation make troubleshooting faster, safer, and reproducible across hosts.

Systematic Troubleshooting

journalctl

Kernel ring buffer; useful for boot and driver diagnostics with timestamps.

What will you adopt first?

narration.text: To wrap up, remember these practical points: use systemctl to check service state and capture its journal entries; filter journalctl by unit and time to find meaningful errors; use dmesg -T for kernel and boot-time clues; inspect processes and sockets with ps and lsof to detect missing daemons or port conflicts; use strace when you need system-call level evidence for obscure failures; and automate diagnostics with Ansible so you can aggregate logs from many hosts. Always document your findings, verify your assumptions with evidence, and prepare a rollback plan before applying changes. These habits convert reactive firefighting into reproducible incident handling and reduce the likelihood of repeat failures. Which diagnostic will you run first when you next see a failed service?
